subject: chemistry
question_text: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of B₂H₆ + NH₃ on heating.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, IPE STUDY MATERIAL for Jr. Students — Chemistry (2026-27 edition), book p.100, chapter 8 p-BLOCK ELEMENTS : GROUP 13, Very Short Answer Questions question 9(e). Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints no per-step allocation on any answer in this chapter. This book prints no exam-appearance years for this chapter, so appearances[] is empty — the chapter has long been examined, we simply have no sourced years for this question. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Because the question says on heating, both stages are given. Both equations were balanced atom by atom while authoring; for the second, three addition compounds carry B 6, N 6, H 36, and two borazine rings plus twelve H₂ carry B 6, N 6, H 12 + 24 = 36. The overall equation named in the second common mistake, 3B₂H₆ + 6NH₃ → 2B₃N₃H₆ + 12H₂, was balanced the same way and carries B 6, N 6, H 36 on each side. TEMPERATURE NOT ASSERTED FOR THE FIRST STAGE: the book prints 120 °C for the addition compound, and this card deliberately does NOT print that number. The diammoniate of diborane is formed at LOW temperature — heating is what destroys it, and this card's own second stage decomposes it at 200 °C — while the standard figure quoted for its formation is 120 K, so the printed unit looks wrong rather than the digits. The card therefore names no figure for that stage and says only low temperature, which is true on either reading, and a Telangana IPE teacher should settle the exact value. The second stage keeps the book's 200 °C, written as 473 K to match the kelvin used everywhere else in this chapter.

steps.label: The addition compound
lines: Diborane B₂H₆ first adds ammonia NH₃.
At low temperature the addition compound
Boron is electron deficient, so it takes
steps.why: Boron in B₂H₆ has an incomplete octet and ammonia has a lone pair on nitrogen, so the two combine as an addition compound before any hydrogen is lost.
common_mistakes: Writing one NH₃. Two ammonia molecules add to one diborane.
Writing only the overall equation 3B₂H₆ + 6NH₃ → 2B₃N₃H₆ + 12H₂. That equation is correct and it balances, but the question says on heating, so show the addition compound stage as well.
steps.memory_tip: Add first, heat second: the addition compound at low temperature, borazine at 473 K.
steps.margin_note: Write the conditions beside each of the two arrows: low temperature for the addition compound, stronger heating for borazine.

steps.label: Borazine on heating
lines: On stronger heating, at about 473 K,
steps.why: Three molecules of the addition compound carry six boron and six nitrogen atoms, which is exactly two borazine rings; the twenty-four hydrogen atoms left over leave as twelve H₂.
common_mistakes: Writing borazine as B₃N₃H₃. Each of the six ring atoms carries one hydrogen, so the formula is B₃N₃H₆.
Leaving out the hydrogen gas. Twelve molecules of H₂ are released.
steps.memory_tip: Six ring atoms, one hydrogen on each: B₃N₃H₆.
steps.margin_note: The question says on heating, so both stages belong in the answer.

insider_note: The question asks about heating, so write both stages — the addition compound at the lower temperature and borazine at the higher one.
